# TravelBahia

> Independent travel guides to Bahia, Brazil for U.S. travelers: Salvador, Morro de São Paulo, Chapada Diamantina, Itacaré and more — with honest safety tips, itineraries and hand-picked pousadas.

TravelBahia (https://travelbahia.com) is an independent English-language travel guide to the state of Bahia in northeastern Brazil, written for travelers from the United States. Content is dated, first-hand, and safety/visa/health information is checked against official U.S. and Brazilian sources.

## Destinations
- [Salvador](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/salvador/): Brazil’s first capital, where Africa, Europe and the tropics meet. Best time: Sep–Mar (dry & sunny). Ideal stay: 3–4 days.
- [Morro de São Paulo](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/morro-de-sao-paulo/): A car-free island of numbered beaches, natural pools and sunsets. Best time: Sep–Mar; low tide for pools. Ideal stay: 3–5 days.
- [Chapada Diamantina](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/chapada-diamantina/): Table-top mountains, blue caves and Brazil’s wildest waterfalls. Best time: Apr–Oct hiking; Dec–Mar fullest falls. Ideal stay: 4–7 days.
- [Itacaré](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/itacare/): Surf beaches tucked into the Atlantic rainforest. Best time: Sep–Mar; surf all year. Ideal stay: 3–4 days.
- [Praia do Forte](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/praia-do-forte/): Sea turtles, natural pools and easy luxury an hour from Salvador. Best time: All year; whales Jul–Oct. Ideal stay: 2–4 days.
- [Trancoso](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/trancoso/): Bohemian chic on a clifftop square above endless beaches. Best time: Sep–Mar; New Year is peak. Ideal stay: 3–5 days.
- [Boipeba](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/boipeba/): Morro’s quieter sister — empty beaches and the Moreré pools. Best time: Sep–Mar; low tide. Ideal stay: 2–3 days.
- [Maraú Peninsula](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/marau-peninsula/): Taipu de Fora’s reef pools and a lagoon-laced wilderness. Best time: Sep–Mar; low tide days. Ideal stay: 3–4 days.
- [Abrolhos](https://travelbahia.com/destinations/abrolhos/): Humpback whales and Brazil’s first marine park. Best time: Jul–Nov for whales. Ideal stay: 1–2 days.

## Guides
- [A Beach Day in Bahia Like a Local: Umbrellas, Fried Cheese & Tides](https://travelbahia.com/blog/beach-day-in-bahia-like-a-local/): Rent an umbrella — about R$10 a day is fair, and anything over R$20 isn’t worth it. Bargain with beach vendors, try the fried cheese, and check the tide before you go because high and low tide change everything for swimming and snorkeling. Never leave your things alone on a public beach: take a floating waterproof bag into the water with your phone, keys and money.
- [Traveling Brazil by Bus: Why You Should Always Book Leito](https://travelbahia.com/blog/brazil-by-bus-leito/): Buses are a good way to travel between Brazilian states. Whenever possible, book a leito seat — it’s like a small individual bed that reclines almost flat, so you can actually sleep on overnight trips. Buses stop at stations every few hours, and some stations even have showers.
- [Markets, Bargaining & Prices in Brazil: What Things Really Cost](https://travelbahia.com/blog/markets-bargaining-prices-brazil/): Street fairs are hugely popular in Brazil — look for hippie markets (feira hippie) and a city’s Mercado Central for food and crafts. Bargaining is expected at markets and with anyone who isn’t an official store. Handicrafts and food are much cheaper than in the U.S., while designer and high-quality items cost about the same as in Europe.
- [Is Bahia Safe for American Tourists? An Honest 2026 Guide](https://travelbahia.com/blog/is-bahia-safe-for-american-tourists/): Yes — Bahia is visited safely by millions of travelers each year, but Salvador requires big-city street smarts. The biggest risk is opportunistic phone and bag theft, not violence against tourists. Keep valuables out of sight, use Uber or 99 at night, stay in busy areas, and you’ll avoid almost every problem. Beach towns like Morro de São Paulo, Praia do Forte and Trancoso feel noticeably more relaxed.
- [How to Get from Salvador to Morro de São Paulo (Catamaran, Ferry or Flight)](https://travelbahia.com/blog/salvador-to-morro-de-sao-paulo/): You have three options: the direct catamaran from Salvador’s Terminal Náutico (about 2–2.5 hours, can be rough), the semi-terrestre route of ferry + road + speedboat via Valença (about 3.5–4 hours, calmer), or a small plane (about 25 minutes, priciest). If you get seasick, choose semi-terrestre or fly.
- [Brazil Visa for U.S. Citizens: The e-Visa Explained (2026)](https://travelbahia.com/blog/brazil-visa-for-us-citizens/): Yes. Since April 10, 2025, U.S. citizens need a Brazilian electronic visa (e-visa) for tourism. You apply online through Brazil’s official e-visa portal, pay the fee, upload a passport scan, photo and supporting documents, and typically receive it by email. Apply at least several weeks before departure and always verify current rules with the Brazilian consulate.
- [Best Time to Visit Bahia, Brazil: A Month-by-Month Guide](https://travelbahia.com/blog/best-time-to-visit-bahia/): The best time for Bahia’s beaches is September through March, when it’s sunny and warm. April to July is the coastal rainy season (May is wettest), though showers are often short. Carnival is in February or early March, humpback whales visit July to November, and Chapada Diamantina is best for hiking April to October.
- [8 Breathtaking Natural Pools in Bahia (and When to See Them)](https://travelbahia.com/blog/natural-pools-bahia/): Bahia’s natural pools form when coral reefs trap warm, clear water at low tide. The most spectacular are Taipu de Fora (Maraú Peninsula), Moreré (Boipeba), Garapuá and Quarta Praia (Morro de São Paulo), Papa-Gente (Praia do Forte) and Recife de Fora (Porto Seguro). Go within a couple of hours of low tide, ideally around full or new moon.
- [Chapada Diamantina Hiking Guide: Waterfalls, Blue Caves & the Vale do Pati](https://travelbahia.com/blog/chapada-diamantina-hiking-guide/): Base yourself in Lençóis for 4–7 days. Don’t miss sunset on Morro do Pai Inácio, the top of Cachoeira da Fumaça, the blue-lit caves of Poço Azul and Poço Encantado, and — if you have time — the 3–5 day Vale do Pati trek. Hire accredited local guides; April to October is best for hiking.
- [What We Ate, Drank & Cooked in Bahia (Honest Picks)](https://travelbahia.com/blog/what-to-eat-in-bahia/): Brazil has some of the best beef, seafood and fruit we have ever eaten — so we cooked a lot ourselves. On the beach, don’t miss fried cheese. In Salvador, try acarajé and moqueca. Ice-cold beer is everywhere because the heat demands it. Caipirinhas were a hit, Pitu (a cachaça) is worth a taste, and we personally didn’t like Catuaba at all.
- [The Perfect 10-Day Bahia Itinerary for First-Time Visitors](https://travelbahia.com/blog/bahia-10-day-itinerary/): Spend days 1–3 in Salvador (Pelourinho, Barra, Rio Vermelho), days 4–7 in Morro de São Paulo with the island boat tour to Boipeba and Garapuá, then choose days 8–10 in Chapada Diamantina for hiking or Itacaré for surf and rainforest before flying home from Salvador.

## Where to stay
- [Where to Stay in Morro de São Paulo: Which Beach Is Right for You](https://travelbahia.com/stays/where-to-stay-morro-de-sao-paulo/): From refined boutique pousadas to charming guesthouses tucked into the jungle, Morro has a stay for every style. Choose Segunda Praia if you want nightlife on your doorstep, Terceira Praia for the best balance of calm water, restaurants and boat-tour access, and Quarta Praia for quiet, spacious beachfront pousadas. The village center is cheapest but involves steep walks.
- [Where to Stay in Salvador: The Best Neighborhoods for Visitors](https://travelbahia.com/stays/best-boutique-hotels-salvador/): First-timers should stay in Barra for its walkable seafront and easy rides everywhere. Choose Santo Antônio Além do Carmo or the Pelourinho for atmospheric boutique hotels in restored colonial mansions, and Rio Vermelho for food and nightlife.
